name: Gum graft
lead: A gum graft, also called gingival grafting or periodontal plastic surgery, is a family of surgical procedures in which gum tissue is moved or added to cover exposed tooth roots or to thicken a thin band of gum [1]. It is most often performed by periodontists, and the usual reason is gum recession, in which the gum margin has migrated away from the crown and exposed the root surface [1].

Recession can cause sensitivity and may make teeth, particularly the front teeth, look longer, so some patients seek grafting partly or mainly for appearance [1]. The same source notes that untreated recession is not by itself a direct cause of tooth loss and that not all recession requires surgery [1]. In looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion the procedure appears as a hardmaxx-category dental option for gumline aesthetics.

Clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov compare graft techniques, donor-site healing and patient experience, and a 2018 literature review summarised on Wikipedia reported that recession was reduced after most root coverage procedures, with pain at the palatal donor site the most common unwanted effect [1].

paras: A free gingival graft moves a thin layer of tissue from the palate to the recession site, where it is sutured in place; it is often described as a way to thicken thin gums [1].

A subepithelial connective tissue graft takes tissue from beneath the palatal surface and is described in the encyclopedic literature as highly predictable for root coverage with less palatal discomfort than a free graft [1].

Pedicle grafts (lateral or coronally advanced flaps) free gum next to the defect and slide it over the root, which requires enough adjacent tissue and may put the donor area at risk of recession [1]. Processed donor-tissue matrices avoid a palatal wound, and opinions differ on whether they match connective tissue grafts [1]. Platelet-rich fibrin, made from a small sample of the patient's own blood, has also been used to avoid palatal harvesting, although the supporting sources for its benefit are described as weak [1].
Recession on front teeth can make them look long or uneven, and patients may choose root coverage for that reason [1].
Grafts are used to cover sensitive exposed roots and to increase the amount of keratinized gum, including around dental implants [1][4].

The most commonly reported unwanted effects are discomfort and pain, mainly at the palatal donor site during the first week, and these did not affect root coverage results in the review summarised on Wikipedia [1]. Donor-site recession can occur with pedicle grafts, and donor-tissue matrices carry possible healing complications and disease-transmission considerations [1].

A 2018 literature review reported reduced recession after most types of root coverage surgery and called for more research on whether one technique is superior [1]. Registered trials include a study of the effect of keratinized mucosa on peri-implant health after free gingival grafting (completed) [4], a comparison of a gingival unit graft with a free gingival graft using 18-month digital colour analysis (completed) [5], trials of palatal donor-site healing using cyanoacrylate and concentrated growth factor (completed) [6], and a survey of patients' perception and postoperative pain after free gingival grafts (completed) [7]. Other registered trials, such as a technique modification study and an oral-care recovery kit study, were still active or of unknown status when listed [3][8].

card.summary: Surgery that moves gum tissue over exposed roots; used for recession and sometimes for looks, with donor-site pain the main reported downside.
card.aka: Gingival graft, gum grafting, root coverage surgery
card.note: Donor-site pain is the most commonly reported unwanted effect.

quick.overview:
A gum graft covers exposed tooth roots or thickens thin gum by moving tissue from the palate, from next to the tooth, or from a processed donor matrix. It is mainly a periodontal treatment for recession, with a cosmetic side when front teeth look long.

A literature review summarised on Wikipedia reported recession was reduced after most root coverage procedures, and registered trials continue to compare techniques.
quick.mechanism: Tissue is placed over the exposed root and sutured so it heals in place; variants differ in where the tissue comes from (palate, adjacent gum, donor matrix or blood-derived fibrin).
quick.risks: Reported effects are discomfort and pain, mainly at the palatal donor site, plus possible donor-site recession with pedicle grafts and healing or disease-transmission considerations with donor matrices.
